# Education in Nigeria
Nigeria's education system is structured into primary, secondary, and tertiary levels, with a focus on universal basic education (UBE). Primary education spans six years (ages 5–12), culminating in a first school-leaving certificate. Core subjects include Mathematics, English, Christian/Religious Knowledge, Agricultural Science, and one of the three major indigenous languages (Hausa-Fulani, Yoruba, Igbo). Students must pass a Common Entrance Examination (CEE) to gain admission to federal, state, or private secondary schools.
Secondary education follows a 6-3-3-4 system: six years of primary, three years of Junior Secondary (JSS), and three years of Senior Secondary (SSS). Students take the Senior Secondary Certificate Examination (SSCE), administered by the West African Examination Council (WAEC), which is a prerequisite for university admission. The curriculum includes core subjects like English, Mathematics, Economics, Civic Education, and Social Studies, with optional electives in science, technology, and arts.
Tertiary education includes universities, polytechnics, and colleges of education. The government controls most universities, with 43 federal, 47 state, and 75 private universities. Admission to universities requires a minimum of SSCE/GCE Ordinary Level credits and a high score on the Joint Admissions and Matriculation Board (JAMB) entrance examination. The typical duration of undergraduate programs is 4–5 years, with engineering, pharmacy, and law programs lasting 5 years. Private universities are increasingly common, with 9 new private universities approved in 2015 and 20 new ones in 2021.
Vocational education is administered by the National Board for Technical Education and includes National Technical Certificates and Advanced National Technical Certificates. Students can pursue vocational training through technical colleges or apprenticeships, which are instrumental in building practical skills and preparing for employment.
Private and religious schools are common, with fees rising sharply (up to 50–70% in 2024). These schools often offer smaller class sizes, modern equipment, and better learning environments. Religious schools, such as those affiliated with Catholic, Methodist, and Baptist churches, historically were less expensive than private schools.
The system faces challenges including teacher shortages, poor infrastructure, and regional disparities. Female education is improving, though gender-based stereotypes and socio-economic barriers persist. The government has implemented initiatives like the Girls' Education Project to support girls' enrollment and retention. Despite progress, issues such as teenage pregnancy, early marriage, and insecurity in rural areas remain significant obstacles to gender equality.
Nigeria's literacy rate is low, at 62.02% (2018), with regional disparities, especially in the North-East and North-West. The government has prioritized literacy, with initiatives to improve multilingual education and access to resources like books and libraries. The administration of President Bola Tinubu has emphasized functional literacy and digital literacy, with a target of 95% digital literacy by 2030.
The education system is undergoing reforms to improve quality and accessibility, including the expansion of public schools and the promotion of vocational education. However, challenges such as teacher training, curriculum relevance, and funding remain significant barriers to achieving equitable and effective education for all Nigerian students.
